Neophyte
NEE-uh-fite
n. (a new convert; a novice)
Greek neos, new, and phyton, a plant: one newly planted. Webster (1828) enters NEOPHYTE without an etymology note.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A neophyte is one newly come to the faith. Webster (1828) gives three senses: “a new convert or proselyte; a name given by the early Christians to such heathens as had recently embraced the Christian faith”; “a novice; one newly admitted to the order of priest”; and “a tyro; a beginner in learning.” He adds that such converts “were considered as regenerated by baptism,” which records the early church’s belief, not Scripture’s teaching. The New Testament speaks tenderly of the new believer: “As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1Pe 2:2). Paul spoke to the Corinthians “as unto babes in Christ” (1Co 3:1). It also warns against setting a new convert over the church. A bishop must be “Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1Ti 3:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): NEOPHYTE, a new convert or proselyte, the early Christians’ name for recent converts from heathenism; a novice; a beginner.

expand to see more

NEOPHYTE, noun

1. A new convert or proselyte; a name given by the early Christians to such heathens as had recently embraced the Christian faith, and were considered as regenerated by baptism.

2. A novice; one newly admitted to the order of priest.

3. A tyro; a beginner in learning.

Key Scripture

1Pe 2:2 — "As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:"

1Co 3:1 — "And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ."

1Ti 3:6 — "Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil."

Heb 5:13 — "For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe."

Modern Corruption

Neophyte now means any beginner in any field, and its Christian origin as a name for new converts is lost.

expand to see more

Webster’s first sense is ecclesiastical: the early church’s name for heathens newly converted. Today a neophyte is any beginner, at a trade, a sport or a hobby. The word has lost the picture of a soul newly planted in Christ.

Webster also records that such converts “were considered as regenerated by baptism.” That is a report of early belief, not a rule of Scripture. The new birth is the work of the Spirit through the word (1Pe 2:2), and baptism signifies it but does not cause it.
